researchPurpose: Identify a task range whose members share domain concepts and usage semantics, and whose real effects are worth testing with a domain DSL.

hypotheses.statement: Task semantics will predict a reusable DSL boundary better than package shape, directory layout, or topic labels alone.
hypotheses.evidence: Topic and support labels failed on concrete near-neighbors; purpose/operation rules produced a bounded range and survived nine-task challenge with one primary and one secondary revision. This is not accuracy or ecosystem evidence.

hypotheses.statement: Making domain rules explicit may improve completeness and constraint observance, but can increase authoring, runtime, or token cost.
hypotheses.evidence: Manual mappings expose completeness/constraint mechanisms and authoring overhead, but no runtime comparison was executed.

hypotheses.statement: A DSL can organize some professional judgment without pretending that every judgment is deterministically executable.
hypotheses.evidence: Three sourced tasks use bounded judgment contracts with explicit context/result/uncertainty while deterministic checks retain encoded invariants; runtime reliability remains unknown.

recommendation.method: typed domain declaration interpreted into bounded agent context with deterministic preflight/post-transform validators and optional operation adapters
recommendation.strongestObjection: The selected tasks may share only a generic transformation shell, and organized Markdown with the same helpers may be equally effective at lower authoring cost.
recommendation.nextMinimum: Five tasks: narrow schema/validator; obligation ledger/renderer; preservation/completeness validators; ordinary natural-run consumption; deterministic tests followed by helper-matched O/M/MH/DH development comparison.
